mission.title: Digital Communication, Tone and Online Discourse

theory.title: Digital Communication, Tone and Online Discourse
theory.explanation: This mission develops advanced digital communication. Effective C2 communication requires writers and speakers to make purpose, audience, evidence and degree of certainty explicit. Analyse the context before choosing a register; distinguish established information from interpretation; organise complex material so that decisions and qualifications remain visible.
theory.tip: Use precise terminology, attribute claims, qualify uncertainty and make the requested action explicit.

patterns.label: Define purpose and audience
patterns.pattern: Identify what the audience needs to know or decide.
examples: State the decision required before presenting supporting detail.

patterns.label: Support and qualify
patterns.pattern: Connect each claim to evidence and state relevant limitations.
examples: The findings suggest a pattern, although the sample is not representative.

patterns.label: Structure for action
patterns.pattern: Use signposting, headings and explicit ownership.
examples: The recommendation is assigned to a named lead for review by an agreed date.

patterns.label: Review for integrity
patterns.pattern: Check terminology, attribution, tone and consistency.
examples: Distinguish verified outcomes from projected benefits.

content.passage:
A distributed team began using a shared discussion channel to resolve project questions. At first, short messages improved response times. Over time, however, decisions became difficult to locate because several threads covered the same issue and participants assumed that silence meant agreement. A terse reply from a senior colleague was interpreted as criticism, although the sender had intended only to confirm receipt.

The team introduced a simple protocol. Messages requiring a decision began with a clear label; background information was placed in a linked document; and unresolved points were assigned to named owners. Participants were encouraged to state explicitly whether they were acknowledging, agreeing or requesting changes. Sensitive disagreements moved to a direct conversation, followed by a written summary of any decision.

The protocol did not eliminate misunderstanding. It reduced the cost of repairing it. The team recognised that digital communication strips away some contextual cues and that concise writing can sound abrupt when intent is unclear. Good netiquette therefore involved more than politeness: it required making purpose, status and next steps visible.
